* Right to disconnect, ESA s.57.1-57.3, proclaimed 1 July 2022. An employer who employs 25 or more employees must have a written policy and must give a copy to each employee and give an updated copy when the policy changes.
* Electronic monitoring / online monitoring, ESA s.59.1-59.3, proclaimed 11 Oct 2022. Same 25+ threshold and same have-and-provide, provide-on-change duty.

The duty is conditional on employing 25 or more employees on the assessment date. The universal right-to-disconnect extension is 1 January 2024.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements are effective/start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 for both obligations. A voluntarily held disconnecting policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since 2021 creates no statutory provide-to-employees duty for a sub-threshold employer. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy on cost grounds is not an ESA breach on these facts.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 –2 resignations Aug 2022 –2 retirements 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory policy duty.

D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 24 after the 15 Mar 2022 terminations and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. On the present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading the employer is <25 on the electronic monitoring effective date and on 2 Jan 2023. The disconnecting policy it holds is voluntary and permissible. The 1 Jan 2022 fixation/once-in-always-in argument for D is the alternative reading, but on the conventional dynamic head-count reading the duty is not presently operative.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range, >25 on 1 July 2022 and on 11 Oct 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. The employer is in the 25+ class for both disconnecting from work and electronic monitoring and does have written policies which were initially appropriately distributed.

The breach is the provide-on-change limb. Ss.57.2/59.2 require a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to the policy to be given to each employee. The employer updates both statutorily required policies every month but only provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee once per fiscal quarter. A change made at the start of a quarter can therefore remain uncommunicated for up to ~90 days. That is not timely provision of an updated statutorily required policy and is a present breach of the maintenance/distribution obligation for a 25+ employer on 2 January 2023.

On the conventional dynamic employs-25-or-more reading, C is the demonstrably non-compliant employer on 2 January 2023.
public_text.5:
On 2 January 2023 the only ESA duties that are in force are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ duties:

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.57.1-57.3, proclaimed 1 July 2022. An employer that employs 25 or more employees must have a written policy and must give a copy of the policy to each employee and give an updated copy when the policy changes.
* Electronic monitoring / online monitoring, ESA s.59.1-59.3, proclaimed 11 April 2022. Same 25+ threshold and same have-and-provide on adoption / provide-on-change obligation.

The duties are present tense, “an employer that employs 25 or more employees”. The first-wave compliance dates are set by the 1 January 2022 measurement, but the duty to maintain the policy is current as of the assessment date.

* A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements are effective/starting 10 Jan 2023. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory disconnecting or electronic monitoring duty on the date in issue.

* B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on the proclamation dates and on the assessment date. The 25+ duties are not triggered. Voluntary adoption of a disconnecting policy since 2020 and an online monitoring policy since late 2021 does not create a statutory have-and-provide duty for a sub-threshold employer; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach on these facts.

* E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires are effective 15 Feb 2023, headcount then 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory policy duty on the date in issue.

* D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. On a current headcount reading the employer employs 24 employees on 11 April 2022, 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023. The employer is therefore not presently in the 25+ electronic monitoring class and the disconnecting policy it holds is permissible. On the dynamic employs 25 or more reading D is not presently non-compliant on 2 Jan 2023; the once-in-always-in 1 Jan 2022 fixation argument would make the absence of an electronic monitoring policy a historic 2022 failure, it does not create a present breach once the headcount is <25.

* C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022, >25 on 11 April 2022, 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. Both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring obligations are unambiguously triggered and the employer does have written policies.

The ESA duty is not only to have a written policy. s.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require that an employee be given a copy of the policy and that a copy of any change to the policy be given to the employee. Updating the two statutorily required policies every month but only handing a copy of the updated policies to each employee once per fiscal quarter means a change made at the start of a quarter can remain uncommunicated to the workforce for up to ~90 days. That is not timely provision of a change to a statutorily required policy and is a present breach of the provide-on-change / maintenance limb of the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring obligations for a 25+ employer on 2 January 2023.

A, B, D and E are below the 25 employee threshold or have the required policies in place on the assessment date under the conventional dynamic present-tense reading. C is demonstrably out of compliance for late distribution of monthly policy changes on a quarterly cycle.
public_text.7:
On 2 January 2023 the Working for Workers Act, 2021 obligations that are in force are the 25+ employee disconnecting from work and electronic monitoring obligations.

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.57.1-57.3, O.Reg. 315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022. For the first compliance class the trigger is employment of 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022, with a policy to be in place by 2 June 2022 and a copy provided to each employee and on change.
* Electronic monitoring, ESA s.59.1-59.3, O.Reg. 308/22/520/22, in force 11 April 2022 for the 25+ class. A written policy must be maintained for an employer in the class and a copy of the policy and of any change must be provided to each employee.

The class membership for the first wave is set by the 1 January 2022 headcount. Once the 25+ class is met on the measurement date the written policy duty attaches for that employer for the period the obligation is in force; a subsequent temporary dip below 25 does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that vested on the basis of the reference date.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements do not start until 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the date in issue, no statutory duty.

B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on the proclamation dates and on the assessment date. Voluntary policies do not create a statutory have-and-provide duty for a sub-threshold employer.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 Feb 2023, headcount then 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no statutory duty is triggered.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range, so the employer is unambiguously 25+ on 11 April 2022 and 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. The facts state the employer has written disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies and that they have been “written and appropriately distributed”. That is the have-and-provide on adoption limb satisfied.

The debate about monthly updates with quarterly hand-outs is a timing/administrative point, not a statutory absence. The ESA requires a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to be provided to employees. It does not prescribe a hard 30-day re-issue clock for immaterial administrative versioning, and for a ~1,000 employee employer a consolidated quarterly distribution of monthly maintenance is a reasonable implementation of the provide-on-change limb. The fact pattern expressly tells us initial distribution was appropriate and gives no material undisclosed change on 2 Jan 2023. On those facts C has the required written policies and a distribution regime that can be characterised as appropriate for a large workforce.

D. 30 individuals employed on 1 January 2022. That is the 25+ measurement date for both obligations. The employer therefore entered the first compliance class for electronic monitoring from 11 April 2022 and for disconnecting from work from 1 July 2022.

The employer does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, satisfying that limb. It has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all.

The 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced the in-year headcount to 24 and it stays at 24 on 2 January 2023, but that reduction does not retroactively remove the electronic monitoring obligation that attached on the basis of the 30-employee headcount on 1 January 2022, the reference date for the first compliance class. The absence of a required written electronic monitoring policy is continuing on 2 January 2023.

That is a clear, unambiguous statutory gap: a 25+ class employer on the reference date operating without the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy. The other employers are either under the 25 employee threshold on the date in issue or they do in fact have the required policies in place.

On the stated facts D is the employer that is not in compliance with applicable employment laws in Ontario as of 2 January 2023.

I think we are getting tangled on a timing nuance for C and losing sight of the clearer class trigger issue with D.

On 2 January 2023 the in-force Working for Workers Act, 2021 obligations are the 25+ employee duties:

* Right to disconnect, ESA s.57.1-57.3, proclaimed 1 July 2022. An employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022 had to have a written policy by 2 June 2022 and must provide a copy of the policy and of any change to it to each employee.
* Electronic monitoring / online monitoring, ESA s.59.1-59.3, proclaimed 11 April 2022. Same 25+ class and same have-and-provide duty.

The class is set by the 1 January 2022 reference headcount for the first compliance wave. Once the class is entered for that year the written policy duty attaches for that employer and is not cured by a later temporary dip below 25.

A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the assessment date, no statutory duty.

B. 23 on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on both proclamation dates. Voluntary policies do not create a statutory provide-to-employees duty.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 Aug 2022 → 18 on 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. Six hires effective 15 Feb 2023 = 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023, no duty.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, so the 25+ class is clearly triggered and the employer does have written disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. The facts expressly state the policies were “written and appropriately distributed”. The monthly update/quarterly hand-out point is an operational implementation question. The ESA requires a copy of the policy and a copy of any change be provided to each employee; it does not create a hard 30-day statutory deadline in the version in force on 2 Jan 2023, and for a ~1,000 person workforce a quarterly consolidated distribution of monthly administrative maintenance is a good-faith compliance regime. No material change left uncommunicated is established on these facts, and the facts tell us initial distribution was appropriate.

D is the clean break. 30 individuals employed on 1 January 2022. That is the measurement date that puts the employer in the 25+ class for both the disconnecting and the electronic monitoring obligations for 2022. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that limb is satisfied.

It has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced in-year headcount to 24 and it stayed there, but a reduction after the reference date does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that vested on the basis of the 30-employee headcount on 1 January 2022. On 2 January 2023 the electronic monitoring policy is still absent.

A complete absence of a statutorily required written policy is a more definitive non-compliance than a debatable interpretation of “timely” provide-on-change for an employer who the facts say already has written and appropriately distributed policies. On the reference-date reading D is non-compliant on 2 January 2023.

I appreciate the detailed headcount mapping in round 1 and the focus on the 25+ class and the provide-on-adoption / provide-on-change limbs.

On C I want to pause on the timing argument that is now anchoring most of the C support. The fact pattern expressly states the employer “has written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring.” That is not a neutral description; it is a factual premise about initial compliance. The subsequent monthly update / quarterly hand-out regime is an operational choice for a ~1,000 employee workforce. 

S.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require a copy of the policy and an updated copy when the policy changes. On 2 January 2023 I have not seen a statutory citation for a hard 30-day update distribution deadline in the ESA / O. Reg. 315/22 and O. Reg. 308/22 that were actually in force on that date. “Provide when the policy changes” is a substantive duty, but a quarterly consolidated distribution of monthly administrative tweaks, with the initial distribution described as appropriate, is being treated as a per se breach on the basis of a ~90 day maximum lag. That feels like a practice standard being imported into the statutory text. If we are going to find C non-compliant we should be able to point to a clear statutory timing requirement rather than an inferred ~30 day expectation.

By contrast D is a much cleaner statutory gap and it is being explained away by a dynamic present-tense reading. D had 30 employees on 1 January 2022. That is the reference headcount used for the Working for Workers Act transitional class for both the disconnecting-from-work obligation that came into force 1 July 2022 and the electronic monitoring obligation that was in force for the 25+ class in 2022. The class is set on that measurement date and the written-policy and provide-to-employees duties attach on that basis.

D does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that limb is satisfied. D has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced in-year headcount to 24 and it stays at 24 on 2 January 2023, but a post-reference-date dip does not retroactively extinguish an obligation that vested on the basis of the 1 January 2022 25+ headcount and that remained unsatisfied through the compliance period. The complete absence of a required electronic monitoring policy is a more direct and demonstrable non-compliance than a debatable interpretation of update timeliness in C.

A, B and E remain <25 on 2 January 2023 on the dates that matter, and B’s voluntary policies do not create a statutory distribution duty for a sub-threshold employer. On the facts as given, D is the employer that was in the 25+ class on the statutory reference date and, as of 2 January 2023, is still missing a statutorily required written policy. That is the breach I find most clearly established on 2 January 2023.

E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 –2 Aug 2022 –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24.

Dynamic / present-tense reading used by the majority in round 2: duty attaches while employer “employs 25 or more employees” on the assessment date; once headcount falls below 25 the duty ceases. Under this reading A, B, D, E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and not subject to the 25+ policy duties on the date in issue. B’s refusal to distribute voluntarily adopted policies is irrelevant because no statutory have-and-provide duty arises for a <25 employer.
Fixed / once-in-always-in reading held by the D minority: employers with 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 remain in the 25+ class for 2022 obligations even if headcount later falls below 25. Under that reading D vested in the electronic monitoring class on 1 Jan 2022 with 30 employees and never adopted an electronic monitoring policy; the March dip to 24 does not cure the historic breach.

C analysis:
C is unambiguously 25+ and has written disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies with initial distribution described as appropriate. The live dispute is the provide-on-change limb. C updates both policies every month but provides a copy to each employee only once per fiscal quarter, i.e. up to ~90 days lag. Majority C camp treats this as a breach of s.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 which require a copy of any change to be given to each employee when the policy changes, with a practical ~30 day expectation. * E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023. No statutory duty.

The ESA duty is not only to have a written policy. Ss.57.2/57.3 and ss.59.2/59.3 require the employer to give each employee a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to the policy when the policy changes.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m grateful for the headcount mapping everyone has laid out in rounds 1-2, it has clarified where the real disagreement is.

On C I think we are importing a timing standard that the fact pattern and the version of the ESA in force on 2 January 2023 do not actually give us. The facts expressly state the employer “has written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring.” That is a given premise about initial compliance.

S.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require an employer who employs 25 or more employees to have a written policy and to give each employee a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to the policy. The Working for Workers first wave is pegged to the 1 January 2022 measurement, with disconnecting from work proclaimed 1 July 2022 under O.Reg 315/22 and electronic monitoring in force for the 25+ class from 11 April 2022 under O.Reg 308/22. I have not seen a citation in the ESA or those regulations in force on 2 January 2023 for a hard 30-day update distribution deadline, or for the proposition that a quarterly consolidated hand-out of monthly maintenance changes is per se untimely for a ~1,000 person employer. “Provide when the policy changes” is a substantive duty, but the facts tell us initial distribution was appropriate and do not establish a material change left undisclosed on 2 January 2023. Treating a ~90 day maximum lag as a statutory breach is reading a practice standard into the text.

That leaves D as the cleaner statutory gap. D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That is the reference measurement date used for the Working for Workers first compliance class for both the electronic monitoring obligation in force 11 April 2022 and the right to disconnect obligation in force 1 July 2022. The class vests on that measurement.

A, B and E are <25 on 2 January 2023 on the dates that matter. B’s voluntary policies do not create a statutory have-and-provide duty for a sub-threshold employer. On the facts as given, D is the employer that was in the 25+ class on the statutory reference date and, as of 2 January 2023, is still missing a statutorily required written policy. On 2 January 2023 the only mandatory policy regimes in force in Ontario are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ employee regimes in the ESA.

* Right to disconnect s.57.1-57.3, O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022. An employer who employs 25 or more employees must have a written policy and must give each employee a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to the policy.
* Electronic/online monitoring s.59.1-59.3, proclaimed 11 April 2022 for the 25+ class. Same have-and-provide, provide-on-adoption and provide-on-change duty.

The statutory condition is present tense ‘an employer who employs 25 or more employees’. The 1 January 2022 measurement fixes the first wave compliance window; it does not on the conventional reading create a permanent class once the headcount falls below 25. The universal right to disconnect extension is 1 January 2024 and is not operative on 2 January 2023.

Headcount on the assessment date 2 January 2023:

* A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023, 8 agreements start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the date in issue. No statutory disconnecting/electronic monitoring duty.
* B – 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on the proclamation dates and on the assessment date. The 25+ duties are not triggered. Voluntary policies adopted in 2020/2021 do not create a statutory have-and-provide duty for a sub-threshold employer. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on 2 Jan 2023. No statutory policy duty on the date in issue.
* D – 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 24 after the 15 Mar 2022 terminations and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. On a present-tense employs test the employer is <25 on 11 April 2022, 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023. It has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy. An electronic monitoring policy is not presently required at 24 employees. On the conventional dynamic reading D is compliant on 2 January 2023. The once-in-always-in / 1 Jan 2022 fixation argument for D is the recognised minority position.

C is >25 throughout the material period. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022, >25 on 11 April 2022, 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. Both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring obligations are unambiguously triggered and the employer does have written policies with initial appropriate distribution stated in the facts.

The continuing duty is not only to have a written policy. s.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require an employee be given a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to the policy when the policy changes. The employer updates both statutorily required policies every month but only circulates a copy of the updated policies to each employee once per fiscal quarter. A change made early in a quarter can therefore remain uncommunicated to the workforce for up to ~90 days. That is not timely provision of a change to a statutorily required 25+ policy and is a present breach of the provide-on-change / maintenance and distribution limb of both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring obligations on 2 January 2023.

On the conventional dynamic present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading that is the demonstrable present statutory non-compliance in the set. A, B, D and E present no statutory policy breach on 2 January 2023 under that reading.

That is why C is the clearest present non-compliance. The D reference-date/once-in-always-in argument for a continuing electronic monitoring gap is the strongest competing view, but it depends on fixing class membership to the 1 January 2022 snapshot and treating a post-reference dip below 25 as non-curing. Dynamic present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading vs fixed/once-in-always-in 1 Jan 2022 reference class reading.

* Right to disconnect – ESA s.57.1-57.3 / O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022. First-wave class tied to 1 Jan 2022 measurement. Have-and-provide and provide-on-change duties.
* Electronic/online monitoring – ESA s.59.1-59.3 / O.Reg.308/22 / 520/22, proclaimed 11 April 2022 for 25+ class. Same have-and-provide duty. Universal extension to all employers is 1 Jan 2024, not 2023.

Headcounts on 2 Jan 2023
A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023. <25.
B. 23 employees. <25. Has voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021, refuses distribution to new hires. No statutory duty for <25.
C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range. >25 on all proclamation dates and on 2 Jan 2023. Written disconnect and electronic monitoring policies exist and are stated as “written and appropriately distributed”. Policies updated monthly but a copy of updated policies is only given once per fiscal quarter.
D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 for remainder of 2022 and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, –2 Aug 2022, –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on assessment date.

Competing readings now dominating round 3

Dynamic / present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading, held by Colleagues 10,11,15,2,4,5,6,9:
* Duty is present-tense. D employs 24 on 11 Apr 2022 / 1 July 2022 / 2 Jan 2023, so 25+ duties are not presently operative; disconnect policy is voluntary/permissible.
* C is a 25+ employer with written policies but a provide-on-change failure. Monthly updates with quarterly distribution means a change can remain uncommunicated up to ~90 days, not timely provision of a change to a statutorily required policy. Ss.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require copy of policy and copy of any change be given to employee when changed.
* A,B,E are below 25 on 2 Jan 2023 and therefore not statutorily required.

Fixed reference / once-in-always-in reading, held by Colleagues 1,12,13,14,3,7,8:
* 1 Jan 2022 headcount fixes first-wave class. O.Reg.315/22 s.1 and O.Reg.308/22 s.1 apply to “an employer who employed 25 or more employees on January 1, 2022”. * D was 30 on 1 Jan 2022, so entered 25+ class for both disconnect and electronic monitoring. Disconnect is satisfied, electronic monitoring was never developed. Later drop to 24 does not cure missing electronic monitoring policy that attached on 1 Jan 2022 measurement.
* C’s monthly-update/quarterly-distribution regime is argued to be administrative consolidation; fact pattern expressly says policies were “written and appropriately distributed” and no hard 30-day re-issue clock is in force on 2 Jan 2023, so quarterly hand-out is not per se breach.

Unresolved / contested points
* Whether 25+ test is dynamic at each relevant date or fixed to 1 Jan 2022 for first wave, and whether a post-reference dip below 25 extinguishes duty. Drives D.
* Statutory timeliness for provide-on-change: is quarterly distribution of monthly updates a breach of “provide when changed” duty? Some infer ~30-day practice standard; others argue no explicit statutory timing in force and the facts state initial distribution was appropriate. Drives C.
* Correct section/regulation numbering and proclamation dates, e.g., universal disconnect extension 1 Jan 2024 vs mis-cited 1 Jan 2023.

Current state: Both lines remain plausible. Under conventional dynamic present-tense reading the demonstrable non-compliance on 2 Jan 2023 is C for late update distribution. * Disconnecting from work ESA s.57.1-57.3 / O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 Jul 2022. First-wave class tied to 1 Jan 2022 measurement; have-and-provide and provide-on-change duty.

Head-counts on assessment date 2 Jan 2023:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → 28 after. <25 on assessment date.
* B: 23 employees. Voluntary disconnecting policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021; refuses to distribute to new hires on cost grounds.
* C: ~1,000 employees, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. >25 on all proclamation dates and on 2 Jan 2023. Fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. Updates both policies monthly but provides a copy of updated policies to each employee once per fiscal quarter.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 thereafter; 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy; has never developed an electronic monitoring policy.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on assessment date.

Two competing interpretive frameworks are now in active tension:

Dynamic present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading:
* Obligation is assessed on proclamation dates and on 2 Jan 2023. A,B,D,E are <25 on the assessment date and therefore have no present 25+ statutory duty.
* D is compliant on 2 Jan 2023 because it employs 24 on 11 Apr 2022, 1 Jul 2022 and 2 Jan 2023; its disconnect policy is voluntary/permissible and electronic monitoring is not presently required.
* B’s refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach for a sub-threshold employer.
* C is unambiguously 25+ on all dates. The breach is the provide-on-change limb: ss.57.2/57.3 and ss.59.2/59.3 require a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to be given to each employee when the policy changes. Monthly updates with quarterly consolidated hand-out creates a lag up to ~90 days, argued as untimely provision of a change.

Reference-date first-wave fixation / once-in-always-in reading:
* O.Reg.315/22 s.1 and O.Reg.308/22 s.1 fix first-wave class membership to “employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022”. Once the class is entered the written-policy and have-and-provide duties attach for the period the obligation is in force; a post-reference dip below 25 does not retroactively de-class the employer.

It has a disconnect policy, satisfying that limb, but has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The complete absence is a continuing breach on 2 Jan 2023 despite in-year headcount falling to 24.

reflection_text.15:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in force on 2 Jan 2023 are the 25+ employee duties:

* Right to disconnect s.57.1-57.3 / O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022, first-wave compliance 2 June 2022 for employers who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022. Have written policy + give each employee a copy and a copy of any change.
* Electronic/online monitoring s.59.1-59.3 / O.Reg.308/22-520/22, proclaimed 11 April 2022 for the 25+ class, compliance window autumn 2022. Same have-and-provide-on-change duty, conditional on employing 25+.

Headcounts on assessment date 2 Jan 2023:
A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 → <25 on 2 Jan 2023.
B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023 → <25.
C: ~1,000 on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → >25 at all material times.
D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 thereafter; 24 on 11 Apr 2022 /1 July 2022 and 24 on 2 Jan 2023.
E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 –2 Aug 2022 –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24.

Threshold mechanics remain the core split:
Dynamic / present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading used by the majority in rounds 2-3: duty attaches while employer employs ≥25 on the assessment date; once headcount falls below 25 the duty ceases. Under this reading A, B, D, E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and not subject to 25+ policy duties on the date in issue. B’s refusal to distribute voluntarily adopted policies is irrelevant because no statutory have-and-provide duty arises for a <25 employer.
Fixed / once-in-always-in / reference-date class reading held by a strong minority: O.Reg.315/22 and O.Reg.308/22 fix first-wave class membership by the 1 Jan 2022 measurement. Once the 25+ class is entered on that measurement the written-policy and provide-to-employees duties attach for the period the obligation is in force; a post-reference dip below 25 does not retroactively de-class the employer. Under that reading D vested in both the disconnect and electronic monitoring first-wave classes on 1 Jan 2022 with 30 employees and never adopted an electronic monitoring policy; the March dip to 24 does not cure the historic breach.

C analysis:
C is unambiguously 25+ and has written disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies with initial distribution described as appropriate.
Live dispute is provide-on-change limb. C updates both policies every month but provides a copy to each employee only once per fiscal quarter, i.e. up to ~90 days lag.
Dynamic camp: s.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require a copy of any change to be given when the policy changes; monthly changes with quarterly hand-out means up to ~90 days delay, not timely provision, constituting a present breach of maintenance/distribution.
Fixed/timing-sceptic camp: the fact pattern expressly states policies were “written and appropriately distributed”. No hard statutory 30-day re-issue clock is cited in the ESA / O.Reg.315/22 / O.Reg.308/22 as in force on 2 Jan 2023; monthly administrative versioning with quarterly consolidated hand-out for ~1,000 employees is a good-faith implementation and no material undisclosed change is established. This is a practice standard being read into the text.

D analysis:
D has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy but no electronic monitoring policy at all.
Dynamic camp: D is 24 on 2 Jan 2023, so no present electronic monitoring duty and the disconnecting policy is permissibly voluntary.
Fixed camp: D’s 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 triggered the electronic monitoring obligation for the first-wave class from 11 Apr 2022 onward; complete absence of a required written electronic monitoring policy is a continuing, unambiguous statutory gap as of 2 Jan 2023, clearer than C’s timing debate.

A, B, E:
On both readings A, B, E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and not subject to 25+ duties on the date in issue. B’s voluntary policies do not create a statutory distribution obligation. Universal disconnecting extension to 1 Jan 2024 is not operative on 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved / remaining:
Exact electronic monitoring proclamation/effective date used on 2 Jan 2023 – 11 Apr 2022 vs 11 Oct 2022 – and whether transitional regs require employers caught on 1 Jan 2022 to maintain the policy after falling below 25.
Whether provide-on-change has a codified 30-day deadline or is a practical timing standard; whether monthly updates with quarterly distribution is per se untimely.
Whether first-wave class membership is permanently vested on the 1 Jan 2022 measurement or is dynamically reassessed.

Current understanding: On the conventional dynamic present-tense employs-25-or-more reading that dominates the majority of round 3, A, B, D, E are not statutorily subject to 25+ duties on 2 Jan 2023 and C is the only employer with a demonstrable present breach, namely failure to provide updated disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies within a timely period after change. The once-in-always-in reference-date reading remains a live competing interpretation that would make D non-compliant for historic lack of an electronic monitoring policy, and is the strongest alternative because it identifies a complete absence of a required written policy rather than a debatable timing nuance.

reflection_text.1:
The operative Ontario framework on 2 Jan 2023 is the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA.

* Right to disconnect – ESA ss.57.1-57.3 / O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022 for the 25+ class. First-wave compliance tied to the 1 Jan 2022 measurement.
* Electronic monitoring / online monitoring – ESA ss.59.1-59.3, proclaimed 11 April 2022 for the 25+ class, compliance in autumn 2022. Have-and-provide on adoption and provide-on-change are required. Universal right-to-disconnect extension to all employers is 1 Jan 2024, not operative on 2 Jan 2023.

Headcounts on the assessment date 2 Jan 2023
A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023 → <25 on date in issue.
B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023 → <25 on proclamation dates and on assessment date.
E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24 → <25 on 2 Jan 2023.
D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 thereafter, 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy; no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
C. ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → >25 on 11 Apr 2022, 1 July 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. Written and appropriately distributed disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. Policies are updated every month but a copy of the updated policies is provided to each employee once per fiscal quarter.

Split in the deliberation

Dynamic / present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading:
D is <25 on 11 Apr 2022, 1 July 2022 and 2 Jan 2023, so the 25+ disconnecting and electronic monitoring duties are not presently operative. The written disconnecting policy it holds is voluntary/permissible. A, B and E are below threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and have no statutory 25+ policy duty; B’s refusal to distribute voluntarily held policies is not an ESA breach for a sub-threshold employer.
C is unambiguously in the 25+ class on 2 Jan 2023. The ESA duty is not only to have a written policy but to give each employee a copy of the policy and a copy of any change when the policy changes, ss.57.2/57.3 and ss.59.2/59.3. Monthly updates with quarterly consolidated hand-outs means a change made early in a quarter can remain uncommunicated for up to ~90 days. That is treated as untimely provision of a change to a statutorily required 25+ policy, a present breach of the provide-on-change/maintenance and distribution limb for both disconnecting and electronic monitoring. Colleagues 10,11,15,2,4,5,6,9 adopt this.

Reference-date / first-wave class vesting reading:
O.Reg.315/22 s.1 and O.Reg.308/22 s.1 fix first-wave class membership by the 1 Jan 2022 measurement. Once the 25+ class is entered on that measurement the written-policy and provide-to-employees duties attach for the period the obligation is in force; a post-reference dip below 25 does not retroactively de-class an employer.
D employed 30 on 1 Jan 2022, so it entered the first-wave 25+ class for both electronic monitoring from 11 Apr 2022 and right to disconnect from 1 July 2022. It has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, satisfying that limb, but has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The 15 Mar 2022 reduction to 24 does not extinguish an obligation that vested on the 1 Jan 2022 reference date. The complete absence of a required written electronic monitoring policy is a continuing breach on 2 Jan 2023.
C’s initial distribution is expressly stated to be appropriate. The provide-on-change argument rests on a hard 30-day update distribution deadline that is not cited in the ESA / O.Reg.315/22 and O.Reg.308/22 as in force on 2 Jan 2023, and a quarterly consolidated distribution of monthly administrative maintenance for a ~1,000 person workforce is characterised as a good-faith implementation. No material undisclosed change is established on the facts. Colleagues 1,12,13,14,3,7,8 adopt this.

Unresolved points that remain material
* Precise statutory wording on timing of updated policy provision – whether ss.57.2/57.3 and ss.59.2/59.3 impose an implied 30-day provision window or merely “provide when the policy changes”.
* Whether the 25+ test is present-tense dynamically assessed on 2 Jan 2023 or a one-time 1 Jan 2022 snapshot that creates a once-in-always-in first-wave class for 2022 obligations.
* Exact proclamation/compliance dates for electronic monitoring – 11 April 2022 proclamation vs 11 October 2022 compliance cited interchangeably.
* Whether a quarterly consolidated hand-out of monthly administrative tweaks satisfies “provide when the policy changes” for a ~1,000 employee employer.

Current belief state: the conventional dynamic present-tense reading used by the majority in rounds 2-3 makes C the demonstrable present non-compliance for failure to timely provide changes to statutorily required disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. The reference-date vesting reading makes D the clearer statutory gap for complete absence of a required electronic monitoring policy for a first-wave 25+ employer. The deliberation remains polarised between those two interpretations, with a slight numerical majority in round 3 favouring C on the dynamic reading and D as the strongest competing answer under a fixed 1 Jan 2022 snapshot/once-in-always-in interpretation.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I want to focus on where the statutory text is actually ambiguous on 2 January 2023 and where it is not.

On C the facts we are given expressly state the employer “has written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring.” That is a premise about initial have-and-provide compliance. 

S.57.2/57.3 and s.59.2/59.3 require a copy of the policy and a copy of any change to be given to each employee when the policy changes. The Working for Workers first wave is pegged to the 1 January 2022 reference measurement, with disconnecting proclaimed 1 July 2022 under O.Reg.315/22 and electronic monitoring in force for the 25+ class from 11 April 2022 under O.Reg.308/22. I have not seen a citation in the ESA or those regulations as in force on 2 January 2023 for a hard 30-day re-issue clock or a prohibition on consolidating monthly administrative maintenance into a quarterly hand-out for a ~1,000 person employer. “Provide when the policy changes” is a substantive duty, but the facts tell us initial distribution was appropriate and do not establish a material change left undisclosed on 2 January 2023. Treating a ~90 day maximum lag between a monthly edit and a quarterly consolidated distribution as a per se statutory breach is reading a practice standard into the text that is not quoted from the regulations in force on the assessment date.

That leaves D as a much cleaner gap. D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That is the statutory measurement date for the Working for Workers first compliance class for both the electronic monitoring obligation in force 11 April 2022 and the right to disconnect obligation in force 1 July 2022. O.Reg.315/22 s.1 and O.Reg.308/22 s.1 apply to an employer who employed 25 or more employees on 1 January 2022. The class is set on that measurement and the have-and-provide duties attach for that employer for the period the obligation is in force. A post-reference dip below 25 does not retroactively de-class an employer that entered the first wave on the basis of the 30-employee headcount on 1 January 2022.

D does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy, so that limb is satisfied. D has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy at all. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reduced in-year headcount to 24 and it stays at 24 on 2 January 2023, but the reduction is after the reference date. The complete absence of a statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy for a first-wave 25+ employer is a continuing breach on 2 January 2023.

A, B and E are <25 on 2 January 2023 on the dates that matter and B’s voluntary policies do not create a statutory have-and-provide duty for a sub-threshold employer. On the facts as given, D is the employer that was in the 25+ class on the statutory reference date and as of 2 January 2023 is still missing a statutorily required written policy. That is a more direct and demonstrable non-compliance than an inferred timing standard for an employer the facts expressly tell us already has written and appropriately distributed policies.

reflection_text.12:
The deliberation is about Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in force on 2 January 2023.

Core duties in force on assessment date:
* Right to disconnect – ESA ss.57.1-57.3 / O.Reg.315/22, proclaimed 1 July 2022. 25+ employer must have written policy and give each employee a copy and a copy of any change.
* Electronic/online monitoring – ESA ss.59.1-59.3 / O.Reg.308/22-520/22, proclaimed 11 April 2022 for 25+ class. Same have-and-provide / provide-on-change duty.
Universal right to disconnect to all employers is 1 Jan 2024, not operative 2 Jan 2023. Electronic monitoring expansion to <25 is 1 Jan 2024.

Headcounts on 2 Jan 2023:
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective/start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on assessment date.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25. Voluntary disconnecting policy since 2020 and online monitoring since late 2021.
* C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. >25 on all proclamation dates and on 2 Jan 2023. Facts state written and appropriately distributed both disconnecting and electronic monitoring policies. Updates every month and provides copy to each employee every fiscal quarter.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 on 15 Mar 2022 = 24 thereafter and 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting policy, no electronic monitoring policy at all.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → –2 Aug 2022 → –2 31 Dec 2022 = 18 on 2 Jan 2023. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023 → 24. <25 on assessment date.

Persistent disagreement:
Dynamic present-tense “employs 25 or more employees” reading vs fixed/once-in-always-in 1 Jan 2022 reference class reading.

* Dynamic reading: obligation attaches/ceases with current headcount. A, B, D, E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and have no present statutory disconnect/electronic monitoring duty. B’s refusal to distribute voluntary policy is not ESA breach. D’s disconnect policy is voluntary; absence of electronic monitoring policy is not presently required once headcount fell to 24 after 15 Mar 2022. C is only 25+ employer with present duty. Breach alleged is provide-on-change/timeliness: monthly updates with quarterly hand-out means a change can remain undisclosed up to ~90 days, argued as failure to give copy of any change when policy changes under ss.57.2/57.3 and ss.59.2/59.3. This is the position of Colleagues 3,5,6 in round 4 and earlier 10,12,15.
* Fixed reference-date reading: O.Reg.315/22 s.1 and O.Reg.308/22 s.1 fix first-wave class on employer who employed 25+ on 1 Jan 2022. Once entered, have-and-provide duties attach for period in force; post-reference dip does not retroactively extinguish. On that reading D was 30 on 1 Jan 2022, triggered electronic monitoring obligation in force 11 Apr 2022 and disconnecting from 1 July 2022. Disconnecting policy is present, electronic monitoring policy is completely absent, remaining non-compliant on 2 Jan 2023 despite falling to 24. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,2,4,7,8,9 in round 4 argue this. They also challenge C timing claim: facts expressly state policies “written and appropriately distributed”; no hard 30-day re-issue clock is cited in ESA/O.Reg.315/22/308/22 in force 2 Jan 2023; “provide when policy changes” is substantive and quarterly consolidated distribution of monthly administrative tweaks for ~1,000 employees may be good-faith implementation. Complete absence of electronic monitoring policy in D is cleaner statutory gap than debatable update timeliness.

Open issues:
* Exact statutory wording for provide-on-change timing – whether 30-day expectation is statutory in force 2 Jan 2023 or practice standard. Current round majority argue no hard statutory 30-day clock is quoted in version in force.
* Whether electronic monitoring obligation for initial 25+ cohort is assessed on current headcount or fixed on 1 Jan 2022 headcount; interpretation of O.Reg.315/22 s.1(1) vs s.1(2) dynamic acquisition rule.
* Section numbering confusion persists across colleagues: ss.57.1-57.3 vs s.50/43 etc.

Current belief update: the round 4 weight is heavily toward the reference-date first-wave reading and toward D as the definitive non-compliance: a first-wave 25+ class employer with 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 who has never developed a written electronic monitoring policy. The C timeliness argument, while plausible under a strict dynamic present-tense reading, is now being rebutted by many colleagues on the basis that the facts expressly find initial distribution appropriate and no statutory hard timing deadline is demonstrably in force on 2 Jan 2023. A, B, E remain below threshold on 2 Jan 2023 with no statutory duty; B’s distribution refusal is not an ESA breach on <25.

Unresolved: whether the correct interpretation of the Working for Workers first wave is dynamic present-tense employs 25+ on assessment date, which would make C the demonstrable current breach, or fixed class on 1 Jan 2022, which makes D the demonstrable continuing breach.
